questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[X].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{4},\,1\le x\le 5
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

 

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{1}^{5}x\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[X].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{x}{12}+\frac{1}{3},\,1\le x\le 3
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

 

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x\cdot (\frac{x}{12}+\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{12}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{3}}{36}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{6})|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{37}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[X].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}x, & 0<x<1 \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}, & 1\le x<2\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

 

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2-0 \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[X].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}, & 0<x<1 \\ \frac{1}{2x}, & 1\le x<e\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x
$$

 

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{e}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{e}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{e}x\cdot \frac{1}{2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{x}{2}|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{e}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{2e-1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[8X-3].$

$$
f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{9},\,0<x<3
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\text{E}[8X-3]=8\text{E}[X]-3
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}x\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{4}}{36}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[8X-3] & =8\text{E}[X]-3 \\  & =8\cdot \frac{9}{4}-3 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\text{E}[5X-2].$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}1-{x}^{3}, & 0<x\le 1, \\ \frac{1}{8}, & 1\le x<3.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the properties of the expected value:

$$
\text{E}[5X-2]=5\text{E}[X]-2
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{3}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot (1-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}x\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{x}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{5})-0+(\frac{9}{16}-\frac{1}{16})-0 \\  & =\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-2] & =5\text{E}[X]-2 \\  & =5\cdot \frac{4}{5}-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\textrm E[X].$

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{9}, \quad 0 \leq x \leq 3
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \int_S x \cdot f(x) \, \textrm dx
$$

 

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{3}x\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{4}}{36}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

We compute the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{0}^{3}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}x\cdot (\frac{x}{2}-\frac{3}{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{x}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{3}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{3x}{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}|}_{0}^{2}+{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}-\frac{3{x}^{2}}{8})|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{31}{24} \\  & =\frac{43}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with the following probability density function, compute $\textrm E[7X-4].$

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3x^2}{7}, \quad 1 <        x <        2
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we simplify using the properties of expected value:

$$
\textrm E[7X-4] = 7 \textrm E[X] - 4
$$

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \int_S x \cdot f(x) \,\textrm{d}x
$$

So, we calculate the expected value of $X$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{S}x\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}x\cdot \frac{3{x}^{2}}{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{3{x}^{3}}{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{3{x}^{4}}{28}|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{45}{28}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[7X-4] & =7\text{E}[X]-4 \\  & =7\cdot \frac{45}{28}-4 \\  & =\frac{29}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **expected value** (also known as the **expectation** or **mean**) of a continuous random variable is the average value we'd expect to get if we observed the random variable many times.

For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the expected value using the following formula:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \int_S x \cdot f(x) \, \textrm dx
$$

 

For example, consider the continuous random variable $X$ with the following probability density function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{x}{4}, \quad 1 < x < 3
$$

We compute the expected value as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x\cdot \frac{x}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{12}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$
